content: Blackwater fever, also known as malignant tertian malaria, is a severe complication of malaria. It is characterized by intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and kidney failure. The condition is primarily caused by heavy parasitization of red blood cells by Plasmodium falciparum, although Plasmodium vivax has also been implicated in rare cases. The term Blackwater fever was first introduced by Dr. John Farrell Easmon, a physician in Sierra Leone, in his 1884 pamphlet titled Blackwater Fever. Dr. Easmon was also the first to treat cases of this condition following the publication of his work. Pathophysiologically, the disease involves the destruction of red blood cells, leading to the release of hemoglobin into the bloodstream. This free hemoglobin damages the glomeruli in the kidneys and subsequently leaks into the urine, where it causes further damage to the renal tubules. The presence of hemoglobin in the urine results in its characteristic dark discoloration, often described as raven black. The most likely explanation for the development of Blackwater fever is an autoimmune reaction triggered by the interaction between the malaria parasite and the use of quinine. The exact cause of the hemolytic crises in Blackwater fever remains unknown, though intravascular hemolysis is a central feature. The condition is most commonly associated with Plasmodium falciparum infections, but at least one case has been attributed to Plasmodium vivax. Epidemiologically, Blackwater fever is much less common today than it was prior to 1950. This decline may be related to the reduced use of quinine for malaria prophylaxis, as quinine is thought to play a role in triggering the condition. However, quinine remains an important drug for the treatment of malaria. Blackwater fever is a serious complication of malaria, though it has a lower mortality rate compared to cerebral malaria. Common symptoms include chills with rigor, high fever, jaundice, vomiting, rapidly progressive anemia, and dark red or black urine. Treatment for Blackwater fever involves antimalarial chemotherapy, intravenous fluid administration, and supportive care. In severe cases, intensive care and dialysis may be required to manage complications and support kidney function.
